QR Code Best Practices: A Complete Guide

A QR code that looks fine on screen can still fail to scan in the real world. This guide covers the practical details that make the difference between a code that works every time and one that frustrates people.

1. Choose the right content type

Use a URL QR code when you want to send people to a live web page, and a text QR code when the message itself is the destination — no website needed.

2. Keep contrast high

Dark modules on a light background scan far more reliably than inverted or low-contrast color schemes. Stick to black on white unless you've tested the alternative thoroughly.

3. Leave a quiet zone

QR scanners rely on a blank margin around the code to detect its edges. Don't crop the code tightly or place it flush against other graphics.

4. Size it for the scanning distance

A code scanned from a phone held a few inches away can be small. A code on a billboard or poster meant to be scanned from several feet away needs to be proportionally larger.

5. Use higher error correction for printed codes

Printed materials get creased, smudged, or partially covered. Higher error correction lets the code still scan even if part of it is damaged or obscured.

6. Always test before mass printing

Scan the exact file you plan to print, at the exact size, with more than one phone and scanner app, before committing to a large print run.

7. Keep the encoded content short

The more data a QR code stores, the denser its pattern becomes, which makes it harder to scan reliably. Shorter URLs and shorter text produce cleaner, more scannable codes.
